t:
The Congress makes the following findings:

    (1) Basic research in imaging, bioengineering, computer science, informatics, and related fields is critical to improving health care but is fundamentally different from the research in molecular biology on which the current national research institutes at the National Institutes of Health (“NIH”) are based. To ensure the development of new techniques and technologies for the 21st century, these disciplines therefore require an identity and research home at the NIH that is independent of the existing institute structure. 
    (2) Advances based on medical research promise new, more effective treatments for a wide variety of diseases, but the development of new, noninvasive imaging techniques for earlier detection and diagnosis of disease is essential to take full advantage of such new treatments and to promote the general improvement of health care. 
    (3) The development of advanced genetic and molecular imaging techniques is necessary to continue the current rapid pace of discovery in molecular biology. 
    (4) Advances in telemedicine, and teleradiology in particular, are increasingly important in the delivery of high quality, reliable medical care to rural citizens and other underserved populations. To fulfill the promise of telemedicine and related technologies fully, a structure is needed at the NIH to support basic research focused on the acquisition, transmission, processing, and optimal display of images. 
    (5) A number of Federal departments and agencies support imaging and engineering research with potential medical applications, but a central coordinating body, preferably housed at the NIH, is needed to coordinate these disparate efforts and facilitate the transfer of technologies with medical applications. 
    (6) Several breakthrough imaging technologies, including magnetic resonance imaging (“MRI”) and computed tomography (“CT”), have been developed primarily abroad, in large part because of the absence of a home at the NIH for basic research in imaging and related fields. The establishment of a central focus for imaging and bioengineering research at the NIH would promote both scientific advance and United States economic development. 
    (7) At a time when a consensus exists to add significant resources to the NIH in coming years, it is appropriate to modernize the structure of the NIH to ensure that research dollars are expended more effectively and efficiently and that the fields of medical science that have contributed the most to the detection, diagnosis, and treatment of disease in recent years receive appropriate emphasis. 
    (8) The establishment of a National Institute of Biomedical Imaging and Bioengineering at the NIH would accelerate the development of new technologies with clinical and research applications, improve coordination and efficiency at the NIH and throughout the Federal Government, reduce duplication and waste, lay the foundation for a new medical information age, promote economic development, and provide a structure to train the young researchers who will make the pathbreaking discoveries of the next century.

fable.w: The tempting reading is that the references to a "central coordinating body" and coordination signal participation. That fails because the section is only a set of congressional findings that requires no process, and the coordination it describes is among federal departments and agencies, all inside the federal government. No outside party (states, experts, the public) is consulted, given a hearing, placed on an advisory body, or granted a right to sue.
fable.s: A number of Federal departments and agencies support imaging and engineering research with potential medical applications, but a central coordinating body, preferably housed at the NIH, is needed to coordinate these disparate efforts

qwen_block.w: This section consists entirely of legislative findings and policy justifications for establishing a new institute within the NIH. It does not contain any procedural requirements for the federal government to consult with, coordinate with, or receive input from parties outside the federal government (such as the public, states, or private entities) before making a decision. The mention of 'coordination' refers to internal federal agency coordination, which is explicitly excluded from the definition of participation.
qwen_block.s: The Congress makes the following findings:
qwen_block.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that the findings mention "coordination" and "underserved populations," implying some form of public or inter-agency participation. However, these are merely legislative justifications for creating a new institute, not procedural requirements for outside parties to participate in decision-making. The text contains no mandates for public comment, advisory boards with non-federal members, or consultation with states/tribes. It is purely a statement of policy rationale.

opus.w: This section is only congressional findings explaining why a new NIH institute should be created. It sets up no comment period, hearing, outside advisory body, consultation with non-federal parties, or right to sue. The one tempting part is the call for a "central coordinating body," but that body would coordinate federal departments and agencies with each other. All of those actors are inside the federal government, so this is not participation.
opus.s: A number of Federal departments and agencies support imaging and engineering research with potential medical applications, but a central coordinating body, preferably housed at the NIH, is needed to coordinate these disparate efforts

qwen_chat.w: The section consists entirely of congressional findings regarding the need for a new institute at the NIH. It describes the benefits of such an institute and the current state of research but does not mandate any consultation, public comment, or coordination with entities outside the federal government. The mention of coordinating federal efforts refers to intra-governmental coordination, which is explicitly excluded from the definition of participation.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that the findings mention "coordination" and "transfer of technologies," which could imply participation. However, these are statements of fact or policy goals regarding internal federal agency coordination (between Federal departments and agencies), not a requirement for the federal government to consult with outside parties before making a decision. The text is purely declarative findings by Congress.
